title: Rice Black Bug: Outbreaks, Bugburn and How to Manage It
metaTitle: Rice Black Bug: Bugburn Symptoms and How to Control It
metaDescription: The rice black bug hit Palawan in 1979, then Mindanao and the Visayas. Learn to spot bugburn, time light traps with the full moon, and manage it.
excerpt: The rice black bug, Scotinophara coarctata, is a dark stink bug that hides at the base of the rice hill by day and sucks sap from the stems. PhilRice calls it itim na atangya, and many farmers say alitangya. A heavy attack burns whole patches of palay reddish brown, so it pays to catch it early.

blocks.text: What the rice black bug looks like

The adult is an oval, dark, almost black stink bug about 8 to 9 millimeters long. Some reports call it the black rice bug or the Malayan black bug. By day, adults and nymphs crowd at the base of the plant just above the water. At night or on cloudy days they climb up the plant to feed higher. Disturb them and they give off a foul smell.

Do not confuse it with the [rice bug](/problems/rice-bug), the slender, long legged atangya that feeds on milky grains in the panicle. The black bug insect is broad and oval, and it works lower down, on the stems and leaf sheaths.
Life cycle and hosts

A female lays about 200 eggs in her life, in masses of 40 to 60 on the lower leaves or the base of the plant near the water. She stands guard over them until they hatch. The eggs start greenish and turn pink as they mature, and they hatch in about a week or less. Nymphs pass through five stages and become adults in about six weeks.

Rice is its main host, but it also lives on corn, gabi, grasses, sedges and broadleaf weeds. The adult flies weakly. Even so, boats and vehicles have carried it over long distances.
How the black bug spread across the Philippines

PhilRice records the first attack in Bonobono, Bataraza, in southern Palawan in September 1979. A major outbreak followed from March to June 1982 and spread to central and northern Palawan, covering 4,500 hectares. A provincial Task Force Black Bug sprayed heavily, but the bugs kept spreading. PhilRice suggests that the spraying wiped out the native natural enemies.

In 1989 a PhilRice task force finally slowed it with the tolerant variety IR1314, releases of parasitic wasps and strict quarantine. Mindanao, the Visayas and later Luzon followed.

blocks.text: PhilRice has since warned of black bug attacks in Central Luzon. The lesson from Palawan and Mindanao still holds. According to PhilRice, numbers only started to fall in the mid 1990s in areas where farmers planted at the same time.
Symptoms: deadheart, whiteheads and bugburn

items: **Deadheart** at tillering: the center leaves of a tiller turn brown and die.
**Whiteheads and empty panicles** at booting: panicles come out partly or not at all, and the grains stay unfilled.
**Bugburn** from maximum tillering to harvest: leaves turn reddish brown and whole patches dry up.
**Stunting and fewer tillers**, with yellowing or reddish brown leaves.

blocks.text:
Two checks help you name the culprit. Stem borers also cause deadhearts, but a stem borer deadheart pulls out easily while a black bug deadheart stays firm at the base. Bugburn also looks like hopperburn from the [brown planthopper](/problems/brown-planthopper). Yet bugburn leaves no honeydew or sooty mold at the base of the plant.

IRRI and PhilRice say ten adults per hill can cut yield by up to 35 percent. During outbreaks, PhilRice recorded losses of 60 to 80 percent. Heavy damage usually shows only after heading, so do not wait for bugburn before you act.
What makes rice black bugs multiply

items: Rice after rice in irrigated areas, and poorly drained fields
Staggered planting, so a young crop is always nearby
Dense planting and too much nitrogen
Weeds and other hosts that feed the bugs between crops
Dry season crops, where IRRI sees damage more often

blocks.text: The moon matters too. Black bug flight follows the lunar cycle, and on full moon nights large swarms fly to lights. That is why swarms sometimes gather around lamp posts and houses near rice areas.
How to manage the rice black bug
Before and during planting

items: **Plant in sync.** Plant varieties of the same maturity within a month of your barangay's regular planting time, ideally over a radius of about 1 kilometer. This breaks the bug's life cycle.

**Use tolerant varieties.** PhilRice lists IR1314 and IR44526 as tolerant, because they replace lost tillers. Plant IR1314 only where tungro is not a problem, since it is highly susceptible to tungro. See [rice varieties in the Philippines](/crops/rice-varieties-philippines) and ask your Municipal Agriculture Office for current choices.
**Consider direct seeding.** Direct seeded rice makes fewer tillers per hill, which leaves the bugs exposed to sun and predators.
**Keep weeds down** in the field and on the bunds, because weeds feed the bugs between crops.
**Go easy on nitrogen.** Excess [urea fertilizer](/blog/urea-fertilizer) favors the pest, so apply the recommended rate in splits.

blocks.text: During the season

items: **Count at the base.** Pick 20 hills at random across the field and count the eggs, nymphs and adults at the base of the plants. It is slow work, but it shows what is really in your field.
**Raise the water.** PhilRice advises raising the water to 8 to 10 centimeters for one to two days to stop eggs from hatching. Eggs kept under water for 24 hours do not hatch.
**Check the eggs first.** Put about 5 egg masses in a container covered with nylon mesh and wait a week. If wasps come out, the eggs are parasitized, and flooding would kill those helpful wasps too.
**Let ducks in.** Ducks eat black bugs. Herd them into insecticide free fields with standing water from about a month after transplanting up to heading.

**Protect natural enemies.** The tiny wasp Telenomus triptus parasitizes the eggs, and the fungus Metarhizium anisopliae kills nymphs and adults. Spiders, crickets, lady beetles, ground beetles and red ants help too.

blocks.text: Light traps and the full moon

Black bugs fly strongly to bright light. PhilRice advises light trapping every night from five days before to five days after the full moon, from 8 PM to midnight. During outbreaks they suggest lamps of 2,000 to 3,000 watts. Bury the bugs you catch in a pit. After harvest, keep the lights on for a few nights, because the adults leave harvested fields in search of food.

Keep the limits in mind. Light traps catch mostly females that have already laid their eggs. So a big catch tells you the bugs are flying in your barangay, not how many sit in your own field. Use the trap as a community warning and the 20 hill count to decide.

In anee.io you can add the light trap nights around each full moon as tasks on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the whole team sees them. Anee, the [AI technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician), can also look at a photo of the bugs at the base of your hills and answer in Tagalog or English.
After harvest
Cut the plants down to the base, then plow and flood the field right away. This kills the adults, nymphs and eggs that hide in the stubble.
Insecticides

PhilRice warns that insecticides alone give only temporary relief, cost a lot and harm other organisms. The Palawan campaign proved it. If your technician still advises a spray, pick an FPA registered product whose label lists black bug on rice.

Two Syngenta examples list black bug on rice on their Philippine product pages: Karate 2.5 EC, with lambda cyhalothrin, and Virtako 40 WG, with chlorantraniliprole and thiamethoxam. Use them only as examples, follow the label, and read our guide to [Alika, Virtako and Chess](/blog/rice-insecticides-alika-virtako-chess).

blocks.title: Work as a barangay
blocks.text: Synchronous planting, light traps and plowing after harvest work best when the whole area does them together. Raise it at your irrigators association or barangay meeting before the season starts.

blocks.text: Rice black bug questions

items.q: What is the rice black bug called in Tagalog?
items.a: PhilRice uses itim na atangya. Many dictionaries and news reports use alitangya. Plain atangya usually means the slender rice bug, so check the insect itself.

items.q: Why do black bugs swarm around lights at full moon?
items.a: Their flight follows the lunar cycle. On full moon nights large numbers of adults fly to light sources, which is why PhilRice times light traps from five days before to five days after the full moon.

items.q: How do I tell bugburn from hopperburn?
items.a: Look at the base of the plants. Hopperburn from planthoppers comes with honeydew and sooty mold. Bugburn from black bugs does not, and you will find the dark bugs themselves at the base.

items.q: Can I control rice black bugs without insecticide?
items.a: Yes, in many cases. Synchronous planting, flooding egg masses, ducks, light traps, Metarhizium fungus and clean bunds together keep numbers down. PhilRice recommends keeping insecticide use to a minimum.
PhilRice lists tolerant lines such as IR1314 and IR44526 that recover by making new tillers. Ask your Municipal Agriculture Office which varieties suit your area.
